metadata.title: Claude, By the Numbers
metadata.subtitle: The Data Plugin
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: what's actually in the spreadsheet you never open, and what does routing that question through a language model actually change? Lands the carry-out that the plugin turns the file into a five-minute conversation, but the answer is only as trustworthy as your data and your assumptions.

beats.narration_text: The assumption: reading a year of revenue means learning spreadsheet formulas. It doesn't. Point a model at the file and ask in plain English. Question is — what's actually sitting in the file you never open?

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. Solo operators don't avoid the numbers — they avoid the tool sitting between themselves and the numbers. A folder called Finances, twelve months of revenue inside it, never opened. Because opening it means writing a formula, and a formula forces you to encode the question in the spreadsheet's grammar. Get the grammar wrong and you can't tell whether the answer is wrong.

The loop is diagnostic. Export a CSV, open it, stare at rows and columns, register a vague up or down, close the file. Nothing was answered because the tool doesn't answer questions — it stores numbers. So the questions that matter go unasked, not because they're unanswerable but because the interface made asking feel expensive. Decisions ride on gut feel.

Change the interface. Point Claude at the same file and phrase it the way you'd phrase it to a colleague: which clients bring in the most revenue, and has the mix changed over the last two quarters? The question no longer has to become a formula first.

No formula, no pivot table. Under the hood: the model reads the columns, infers what you meant, runs the analysis, translates the result back into a sentence. The design choice — hide the machinery, keep the input in English. It buys speed; it costs you sight of the exact query.

That's natural-language querying. What were total sales by month? Which client led last quarter? Am I spending more on software than six months ago? Each of those gets translated into a specific operation — a group-by, a rank, a period comparison — and returned as a sentence rather than a table. Same underlying operations, different surface.

production_viz.label: ASK IT LIKE A QUESTION
production_viz.caption: a sentence back, not a table

beats.narration_text: This is the mechanism paying off. 'I think business is going okay' — that's vibes. Three clients carry sixty percent of revenue, one of them sliding since September — that's a specific claim you can act on. The gap between the two isn't intelligence, it's whether the question got asked at all.

Beyond a single answer, the plugin has four modes: exploration, cleaning, visualization, comparison. Not every question needs all four. Together they cover the pipeline from raw export to something you'd trust enough to act on.

Exploration first. Point Claude at a mystery export — column headers that don't quite make sense — and it describes the structure, flags outliers, and suggests the questions worth asking. The design choice worth naming: the tool proposes questions rather than waiting for one. The best question is often not the one you started with.

production_viz.label: EXPLORE
production_viz.caption: the best question isn't always the first one

beats.narration_text: Cleaning. Messy data is the default — inconsistent date formats, duplicate rows, impossible values like negative sales. The plugin does the tedious work and reports exactly what it changed. That report matters more than the cleanup itself: automation without a change-log is just moving the trust problem sideways.

Visualization. Ask for monthly revenue over the past year and you get a chart back — for a deck, a partner, or just to see your own trajectory. Line for trends, bars for comparisons. The optimization: pick a sensible default and let you override it, rather than forcing a chooser up front.

production_viz.label: VISUALIZE
production_viz.caption: for a deck, or just for you

beats.narration_text: Comparison. How does this quarter stack against last? Is acquisition cost climbing or falling? Totals are a snapshot; comparisons are a derivative — they tell you which way things are moving, which is what a decision actually needs.

production_viz.label: COMPARE
production_viz.caption: totals show where you are; comparisons show where you're heading

beats.narration_text: Every business has a question it's been avoiding. Start there. Point Claude at your invoices and your expenses and ask: am I profitable, month to month? Two files, one join on the month, revenue minus cost per row — that's the machinery. What it hands back is a read on financial health, not a spreadsheet.

production_viz.label: THE AVOIDED QUESTION
production_viz.caption: a real read on financial health

beats.narration_text: Five minutes of this beats a year of meaning to look. Make it a ritual: first of the month, ten minutes. Point Claude at last month's revenue and expenses and ask for a health check — total revenue, total expenses, margin, comparison to the month before, and anything that looks off. Same six-part checklist every month; the value is in the repetition, not the phrasing.

production_viz.label: THE MONTHLY RITUAL
production_viz.caption: the review a fractional CFO would give you

beats.narration_text: Do it every month and surprise goes out of the numbers. Each review stacks on the last. The point of the repetition is signal detection: a trend is only a trend against a baseline, and the baseline only exists if you built it.

For a service business, one question dominates the rest: how concentrated is your revenue? Ask directly — who are my top clients, what share rides on the top three, and is anyone quietly spending less than before? That third question is the one most operators skip, because in a spreadsheet it costs three joins.

Concentration is one of the most important things a solo operator can know. A single client at forty percent of your income is a risk shape, not a revenue shape — if you don't see it, you can't plan for the day they leave. The plugin makes that check trivial. What that removes is not the analysis time; it's the excuse for not checking.

The follow-up is cheap. Of those top clients, which are declining? What changed last quarter that might explain it? Cost of the second question is close to zero — same file, same session, same context. That's the design choice paying off. Remember the client sliding since September? This is how you catch that early.

Here's the honest part. The plugin's output is only as trustworthy as two things: the data you fed it, and the assumptions underneath it. Clean inputs plus sound assumptions give a reliable read. Bad inputs give confident, well-formatted nonsense — and confident nonsense is worse than no answer, because it looks like a decision.

That's exactly why it reports what it cleaned. You can verify each fix before you trust the numbers built on top of it. Call the log paperwork and you'll skip it; call it the audit trail and you won't — because auditing is the only way to check that the tool's read of the data matches yours.

Draw the line. The plugin can tell you a client is declining. It can't tell you whether to call them, discount, or let them go. It surfaces the number; you own the decision. The optimization: give the operator faster inputs, not fewer choices.

Four habits make it work. Ask specific — 'analyze my data' is a null request. Iterate — your first question breeds a better one. Compare, don't just total; totals don't decide, differences do. And export on a schedule, because the plugin can only see the data you actually give it.

production_viz.label: FOUR HABITS
production_viz.caption: the habits that make it work

beats.narration_text: The data plugin turns the spreadsheet you're avoiding into a five-minute conversation. But the answer is only as trustworthy as your data and your assumptions. The judgment stays yours.

props.quote: The data plugin turns the spreadsheet you're avoiding into a five-minute conversation — but the answer is only as trustworthy as your data and your assumptions, so the judgment stays yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Give it your invoices file and your expenses file for the year, then ask: tell me what's in each file and flag anything messy — bad dates, duplicates, impossible values — then run a business-health check: am I profitable month to month, which months were strongest and weakest, is any expense growing faster than revenue, and end with the one follow-up question I should ask next. Go deeper: once you have the answer, ask what a change in that top-line number would have to look like before you'd change how you run the business.

llm_exercise.prompt: I run a small business. Here's a spreadsheet of my invoices and one of my expenses for the year. First, tell me what's in each file and flag anything messy — inconsistent date formats, duplicate rows, impossible values like negative sales. Then give me a business-health check: am I profitable month to month, which months were strongest and weakest, is any expense growing faster than revenue. End with the one follow-up question I should ask next.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: once you have the answer, ask what a change in that top-line number would have to look like before you'd actually change how you run the business — that's the difference between reading a number and using one.
